newsitem.title: BELGIUM: JEAN-MARC CONNEROTTE - MAGISTRATE AS FOLK HERO.
newsitem.headline: JEAN-MARC CONNEROTTE - MAGISTRATE AS FOLK HERO.

text.p: Magistrate Jean-Marc Connerotte, who on Monday was kicked off investigations into the paedophile sex abuse and murder scandal that has traumatised Belgium, has gone from virtual unknown to national hero in just two months.

Together with regional public prosecutor Michel Bourlet, the thin, bespectacled philosophy graduate has earned the respect of the general public at a time when confidence in the Belgian legal system is at a very low ebb.
Connerotte's task was to build a balanced case file on which Bourlet would then decide whether to proceed.

The arrest of 13 people, including chief suspect Marc Dutroux, leading to the rescue of two young girls and the discovery of the bodies of four others, has shocked the nation and raised questions about the extent of the child sex ring.

But on Monday Connerotte had the case ripped out of his hands for having accepted a free plate of spaghetti from the Marc et Corine group specialising in helping the parents of missing children. On the plus side, Bourlet remains on the case.
The removal of Connerotte will be deeply unpopular.

The legal manoeuvre by Dutroux lawyer Julien Pierre has already prompted demonstrations around the country in support of the two, as well as a petition with 300,000 signatures. On Monday it was met with howls of derision by protesters,

Apart from Pierre and some other defence lawyers, virtually no one in Belgium wanted Connerotte removed from the case, including the country's top prosecutor Eliane Liekendael who only reluctantly argued that he had compromised himself.

But protestations that the letter of the law left the court with no choice are unlikely to calm a public fever fuelled by conspiracy theories that people in high places are involved in the affair and are trying to cover their tracks.

Connerotte and Bourlet are widely seen as the only honest investigators capable of bringing to a conclusion an affair which has shocked Belgians as much for the bungling work of some investigators as for the horror of the crimes themselves.
It would not be the first time Connerotte had been bounced off a case just when important breakthroughs were made.

Two years ago, after having arrested three key suspects in a case linked to the 1991 Mafia-style murder of Socialist patriarch Andre Cools, Connerotte and Bourlet had the case taken off them and handed to rival investigators in Liege.

Their removal from the case prompted speculation of political interference in the justice system as well as exposing deep flaws in the system itself with different regional prosecutors jealously guarding their own territory.
The three suspects were freed, only to be rearrested last month.

In August, after Dutroux had led police to the bodies of eight-year-olds Julie Lejeune and Melissa Russo, Bourlet -- in prophetic words -- sparked a scandal of his own when he to told television he would finish the case "if I am allowed".
King Albert, echoing those words, spoke of a need to get to the bottom of the affair.
The police in the southern town of Neufchateau where Bourlet and Connerotte are based are also known to want to keep Connerotte on the case. They at least got their way.

Bourlet, an avuncular, greying figure and passionate rose gardner who is supposed to make sure his investigating magistrates in Neufchateau run balanced inquiries, contrasts markedly with his star operative.
Connerotte, a dark, earnest figure and motorbike enthusiast, came to the law from the other side of the barricades.

He was arrested in 1968 during student demonstrations in Leuven where he was at university, and lectured in philosophy in Australia for two years before returning to Belgium where he became a magistrate in Doornik before moving to Neufchateau.
